findings.where: Screen 7 (Inject and clamp) and the feeder tiles
findings.what: Switching to Inject and clamp drops F1's tile from 575 mA to 0 mA even though the 60 Hz charging current still flows; no text or tile label says the locator's clamp reads only the pulse, so the key step behind the lesson's one thing to see is missing.

"Size alone does not find the fault" contradicts the screen's own answer: faulty F1 at 101 mA is still the biggest reading on the board, seven times each 14.4 mA feeder, so the Why should instead say that a feeder's reading depends on the rest of the board, not on whether it is faulty.

Neither says why an 86 mA margin is hard to see when, in the ideal picture, the faulty feeder always reads the most: the step that real clamps carry errors from load current and unequal cables, and that a partial fault shrinks every reading, is skipped.
The dial and the Monitor tile read 0 kΩ with "Hull, now at L1's voltage" right beside a question that says the monitor reads 19.1 kΩ, so the screen contradicts its own question.
The Monitor tile reads 375 kΩ while the question says 2 MΩ, and the picture has no fire pump in it, so the picture contradicts the question and does not show the subject.

There are eight footnotes ([^1] [^2] [^3] [^4] [^8] in explain, [^9] [^7] [^6] in practice), and most sit on explanations, not on values he might look up; keep [^7] (500 V DC) and perhaps [^9], and drop the rest.

"Ship rules ask for at least that on a switchboard" says where the rule comes from, and its "that" points back past the core-to-core sentence; fold the minimum into "Test at 500 V DC or more" instead.

The 60 Hz mode shows only numbers in the tiles, while the pulse mode draws its path, so the cause (charging current returning from the hull through every healthy feeder's capacitance and home through F6's fault) is never drawn.
"Every feeder's capacitance passes charging current" is true before the fault too; the point is that the three charging currents no longer cancel in the clamp.
Both SHOW screens are exactly 90 words, at the limit, and screen 1's "The solid fault is a path of almost no resistance, so the dial reads 0 kΩ, below its 44 kΩ line" runs to 21 words; split it.

findings.where: All five SHOW screens at 360 px
findings.what: The 75 to 90 words of text fill the first phone screen, so the 2 to 3 s demonstration plays out of view and there is no replay; start the timeline when the picture scrolls into view, or offer a replay.

findings.where: SHOW screens, feeder tiles and Tool picker
findings.what: On SHOW screens the tiles can be tapped and the tools switched, but nothing on screen says so; this needs a read-safe sentence.

findings.where: Picture, the pump on F6's sub-board
findings.what: The fault spark inside the pump is about 4 px across at 360 px and is easy to miss, though it marks the thing the whole hunt is for.
F1's long cable run is drawn as a zigzag that reads as a resistor symbol, which is risky in a lesson about insulation resistance; use a coil or a long-cable mark instead.

findings.where: Picture, every feeder tile in the clamp tools
findings.what: The clamp ring touches the start of the capacitance label ("0.05 µF", "2 µF") at both 360 px and 1280 px.
The "Closed" label runs straight into the open-breaker symbol, so it reads as "Closed/Open".
At 0.4 s the Pump running row vanishes and the Test across picker appears without a fade, so everything below shifts in one jump.
"A healthy circuit gives the slow pulse no path to the hull" and "The pulse flows only where the fault is" are absolute, while explain rightly says "next to nothing"; match that wording.
"This picture is simplified. It has one solid fault and ideal clamps." talks about the lesson's own drawing rather than the content; say it as content or leave it to the model notes.

These brief items for lesson 7 are not used anywhere: the DC points (shed loads one at a time, clamp round both poles, inject on one side only) and the common causes (water in junction boxes and deck lights, damaged cables, motors and heaters); one practice line each would cover them.
